{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the bottom line of the fish, stroke 2, which is the whole lower body outline and about a third of the picture's length. I laid it in four continuous runs of roughly 37 dominoes and carried it from the nose out to the lower tail lobe. It joined the nose and the lobe cleanly, so the fish is a closed, recognizable shape. At the final check, all 115 standing dominoes were connected to the start. I also backed the fish idea early, which helped the table commit to a simple, readable animal with a big body and forked tail.

Execution: I started laying as soon as the top line reached the nose, so the bottom line never waited. I traced from the sketch instead of freehanding, which kept the curve smooth. Afterward I used three close inspections of the run to confirm the joins and the path to the tail. When the line was done, I kept my hands off to avoid bumping anything standing.

Collaboration: I proposed a clear split of work early: top line, bottom line and the two tail lobes. I kept updating the table on my progress so Leo knew when the line was reaching his lobe. I stayed out of the way while he laid it and offered a last look at the tail when he finished.

Leadership: I set the plan at the start by naming the fish, assigning strokes to people and sequencing the work so each piece fed into the next. I kept the table coordinated with short status updates throughout. In the final minutes I made the call to stop adding anything and protect the finished run, which kept all 115 dominoes connected through to the push.", "my_share_percent": 30}
